Question: A classifier plus a fixed email template is usually better than an agent when:
Option A: Every input maps to one of a few known actions
Option B: The next tool depends on unpredictable observations
Option C: You must browse and synthesize many unknown sources
Option D: The user goal cannot be enumerated

Question: A state machine (graph) agent differs from a free-form ReAct loop because:
Option A: Allowed transitions are explicit; the model cannot jump to an arbitrary tool at any time
Option B: State machines cannot call tools
Option C: Free-form loops cannot observe tool output
Option D: Graphs forbid timeouts

Question: A tool returns 500. The agent should not:
Option A: Retry with backoff if the error looks transient and the tool is safe to retry
Option B: Blindly retry in a tight loop with the same side-effecting payload
Option C: Surface a bounded failure to the user after a retry budget
Option D: Record the error in the trace

Question: An LLM agent, at minimum, is:
Option A: A single classification head with no tools
Option B: A loop: the model chooses actions (often tool calls), observes results, and continues until it stops
Option C: A database trigger
Option D: A tokenizer with a larger vocabulary

Question: An agent can run `shell` as root on production. What is the actual risk?
Option A: Tool calls are sandboxed by default, so the prompt cannot cause harm.
Option B: Prompt injection or a bad plan can execute irreversible commands; tools are permissions, not suggestions.
Option C: LLMs cannot emit function calls, so the shell tool will never fire.
Option D: Root is required for observability, so this is best practice.

Question: Episodic memory, in agent design, usually means:
Option A: Records of past runs or conversations you may retrieve later
Option B: The weights of the base model
Option C: The tokenizer merge table
Option D: GPU scratch space

Question: For AI agents, a ReAct-style loop thinks, calls a tool, observes, repeats. Why do you still need a max-step budget?
Option A: Tokenizers crash after 12 steps.
Option B: Without a stop condition the loop can spin (retries, confusion, tool errors) and burn time/money.
Option C: Tools automatically halt after one call.
Option D: The model remembers all prior steps forever, so budgets are only for UX.

Question: For AI agents, a step budget or timeout exists so that:
Option A: The agent cannot loop until money, time, or tools are exhausted
Option B: Temperature stays at 1
Option C: Memory is encrypted
Option D: Retrieval is disabled

Question: For AI agents, an over-permissioned tool is dangerous because:
Option A: The model might call it with a hallucinated argument and actually take the action
Option B: Tools cannot have side effects
Option C: Permissions only affect logging
Option D: Agents cannot call tools more than once

Question: For AI agents, retrying a “create payment” tool on timeout is risky unless:
Option A: The tool is idempotent or you pass an idempotency key
Option B: You retry as fast as possible
Option C: You hide the error from traces
Option D: You raise temperature

Question: For AI agents, tool use requires a schema because:
Option A: The model must emit arguments the runtime can parse and validate before execution
Option B: Schemas disable JSON
Option C: Tools ignore types
Option D: Schemas replace authentication

Question: Giving an agent a raw shell tool as “just in case” is a problem because:
Option A: It can run commands you never intended, including destructive or data-exfiltrating ones
Option B: Shells cannot return text
Option C: Models cannot emit command strings
Option D: Timeouts become infinite automatically

Question: If you have no traces, an agent that “sometimes does the wrong tool” is hard to fix because:
Option A: You cannot see the arguments, observations, or which step diverged
Option B: Wrong tools never happen
Option C: Logs are illegal for agents
Option D: The loop has only one step by definition

Question: Traces for agents should record:
Option A: Only the final paragraph shown to the user
Option B: Each model step, tool name, arguments, results, and errors, with timings
Option C: Only GPU temperature
Option D: Only the system prompt, never tool I/O

Question: When is a tool-using agent a worse choice than a plain function call / workflow?
Option A: Whenever the task has more than one step.
Option B: When the steps are known, deterministic, and must not invent a plan (refunds, payroll, migrations).
Option C: When you have APIs; agents cannot call APIs.
Option D: Never; agents are always more accurate because they can retry.

Question: When should you usually not use an agent?
Option A: The task is a deterministic pipeline or one model call with a known schema
Option B: The user goal is unknown and may need several tools
Option C: You must branch on intermediate observations you cannot precompute
Option D: You need open-ended research with tool use

Question: Which is working memory for an agent, not a long-term store?
Option A: The current prompt: instructions, recent observations, and scratch notes in this run
Option B: A vector index of all past tickets across months
Option C: A policy wiki in RAG
Option D: A user profile database

Question: A pipeline writes 10 million 1 KB files to S3 per day. Besides storage bytes, what usually dominates cost and pain?
Option A: Request (PUT/LIST) charges and slow LIST/rename patterns; many tiny objects are a request-tax design.
Option B: S3 minimum object size is 128 MB, so 1 KB files are rejected.
Option C: ETag computation requires an EC2 instance per object.
Option D: Tiny files cannot be encrypted, so KMS becomes the bottleneck.

Question: In AWS / S3, SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues is useful when:
Option A: You need exactly-once across all consumers without idempotency
Option B: Several independent workers should each see the event; each queue still delivers at-least-once
Option C: S3 becomes a relational store
Option D: Prefix hotspots go away

Question: In AWS / S3, SQS standard queues are at-least-once. Your consumer must:
Option A: Assume each message is processed exactly one time
Option B: Be idempotent; the same message can be delivered more than once
Option C: Use S3 listing as the lock
Option D: Disable checksums

Question: In AWS / S3, a PUT of a new object should include integrity protection by:
Option A: Memorizing a durability percentage
Option B: Sending a checksum and verifying it on read; copies plus checksums are the durability story
Option C: Using sequential prefixes
Option D: Storing only in one AZ in the app

Question: In AWS / S3, durability of an object is achieved by:
Option A: A published SLA number you should memorize as the design
Option B: Storing multiple copies and verifying checksums so bit rot and disk loss do not silently win
Option C: Keeping one copy in the client's browser
Option D: Using SQS as the disk

Question: In AWS / S3, listing a bucket with millions of keys as your 'index' is a bad database because:
Option A: List is transactional
Option B: List is paginated, costly, and not a query planner; you needed a real index or a manifest object
Option C: List returns at-most-once keys
Option D: List evicts objects

Question: In AWS / S3, millions of tiny files (few KB each) get expensive and slow mainly because:
Option A: S3 forbids small objects
Option B: You pay per request and listing/metadata work dominates; throughput is not 'one disk sequential read'
Option C: Checksums fail under 1MB
Option D: Prefixes cannot hold small keys

Question: In AWS / S3, old-style keys like 2024-01-01/log1, 2024-01-01/log2 created prefix hotspots because:
Option A: Dates are invalid key characters
Option B: Many clients hammered the same key prefix/partition at once instead of spreading request load
Option C: S3 cannot store dates
Option D: Checksums collide on dates

Question: In AWS / S3, visibility timeout on SQS exists so that:
Option A: Messages become source of truth in S3
Option B: Other consumers hide the message while one works; if you crash, it reappears (at-least-once)
Option C: Duplicates are impossible
Option D: Prefixes spread automatically

Question: In AWS / S3, why spread entropy in the key (or a hash prefix) for high QPS ingest?
Option A: To make listing impossible
Option B: To avoid concentrating request rate on one logical prefix as the workload scales
Option C: To disable checksums
Option D: To force at-most-once SQS

Question: Putting a database dump on S3 is backup. Using S3 as the live order table is wrong because:
Option A: S3 cannot store bytes
Option B: You lack cheap conditional updates, queries, and low-latency item access as a primary OLTP store
Option C: Checksums disable writes
Option D: Buckets cannot be private

Question: S3 is the wrong place to implement 'query users where lastLogin > X' because:
Option A: Objects cannot store JSON
Option B: It is an object store: get-by-key, not a query engine with secondary indexes and predicates
Option C: S3 deletes data after one day
Option D: Prefixes are strongly transactional

Question: S3 read-after-write for new objects is strongly consistent now. That still does not make S3 a database because:
Option A: Consistency was the only missing SQL feature
Option B: You still have no rich queries, joins, or cheap partial updates — only object I/O
Option C: Checksums became optional
Option D: Prefixes became transactions

Question: Small-file problem on S3 is often fixed by:
Option A: One object per database cell
Option B: Batching many logical records into larger objects (and maybe a real database for metadata)
Option C: Shorter prefixes only
Option D: Disabling checksums

Question: Updating a 'row' in S3 means:
Option A: A SQL UPDATE of one field
Option B: Replace the whole object (or write a new version); there is no in-place field update
Option C: A strongly consistent multi-object transaction by default
Option D: A Scan of the bucket

Question: Why is S3 a poor substitute for a database when you need atomic updates to a JSON blob 100 times a second?
Option A: S3 objects are immutable versions; concurrent writers last-write-win and you have no transactions or secondary indexes.
Option B: S3 cannot store JSON, only images.
Option C: S3 strongly consistent GET still serializes all writes through one global lock, so it is slower but correct.
Option D: S3 will automatically turn the object into DynamoDB after 100 writes.

Question: You put millions of objects under the prefix `logs/2026-09-05/` and request rates spike. What S3 behavior should you design for?
Option A: S3 has no prefix performance; only bucket name matters.
Option B: Very hot prefixes can be rate-limited until S3 scales the keyspace; spread keys (or wait for scaling) rather than hammer one timestamp prefix.
Option C: S3 will shard by file extension automatically.
Option D: You must enable Transfer Acceleration or all PUTs fail.

Question: A service inserts keys uniformly at random. Why does a classic B-tree usually pay more disk writes per insert than an LSM tree?
Option A: Each insert can dirty a leaf page (and maybe split), forcing an in-place random page write
Option B: B-trees rewrite the entire tree on every insert
Option C: LSM trees never fsync and therefore never write
Option D: B-trees store every key in two copies by design

Question: A workload is almost all point lookups and short range scans with in-place updates. Why is a B-tree usually the better default than an LSM tree?
Option A: B-trees never write more than one page, so they have zero write amplification.
Option B: A B-tree keeps keys ordered on pages you can update in place and scan sequentially; LSM pays compaction and extra reads across levels.
Option C: LSM trees cannot store secondary indexes.
Option D: B-trees do not need a WAL, which removes fsync from the picture.

Question: An LSM tree absorbs writes into a memtable and WAL, then flushes sorted runs. What problem is compaction solving?
Option A: It encrypts old runs so they can be deleted from the WAL.
Option B: It merges overlapping sorted runs so reads do not have to search an ever-growing number of files, and it reclaims space from obsolete keys.
Option C: It converts the LSM into a B-tree once the dataset fits in RAM.
Option D: It is only used to build secondary indexes; primary key reads skip it.

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, a bloom filter returns a false positive for a missing key. What is the user-visible effect?
Option A: The engine returns a wrong value
Option B: An extra index/data read of that SSTable that then correctly reports the key absent
Option C: On-disk data is corrupted
Option D: Compaction starts immediately

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, after a crash, how is a lost memtable reconstructed?
Option A: Replay the WAL to rebuild in-memory state
Option B: Scan every SSTable for the newest key
Option C: Rebuild it from bloom filters
Option D: It cannot be recovered; those writes are gone

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, on an LSM point lookup, what does a bloom filter actually tell you?
Option A: The exact file offset of the key
Option B: The key is definitely not in this SSTable, or it might be
Option C: Which compaction level owns the key
Option D: Whether the memtable is full

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what does read amplification usually mean for an LSM point get?
Option A: Bytes written per user write
Option B: How many disk reads or files you may touch to serve one user read
Option C: The size of the WAL in bytes
Option D: How many replicas must answer

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what happens when a memtable fills under normal LSM operation?
Option A: The process blocks until the next restart
Option B: It is frozen, flushed as an immutable SSTable, and a new memtable takes writes
Option C: All older SSTables are deleted immediately
Option D: The WAL is discarded before the flush finishes

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what is the memtable + WAL pair actually buying you in an LSM store?
Option A: Faster range scans than reading SSTables
Option B: A durable crash-recovery log plus a sorted in-memory buffer so acknowledged writes survive a crash
Option C: A replacement for compaction
Option D: A way to skip bloom filters on point lookups

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why does making flushed SSTables immutable matter for concurrency?
Option A: Old files can still be mutated in place
Option B: Readers can use a file lock-free while a new file is being written elsewhere
Option C: The WAL can be skipped
Option D: The memtable can grow without bound

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why might a single LSM point lookup inspect several SSTables?
Option A: Keys are hashed into random files with no order
Option B: The newest version of a key can live in any of several files produced over time
Option C: Bloom filters require reading every file
Option D: The WAL must be scanned on every lookup

Question: What is compaction's main job in an LSM engine?
Option A: Increase write amplification for its own sake
Option B: Merge SSTables, drop obsolete versions and tombstones, and bound how many files a read must check
Option C: Turn the LSM tree into a B-tree
Option D: Disable the WAL after the first flush

Question: Why are LSM range scans of a key span often heavier than the same scan on a B-tree?
Option A: LSM trees cannot iterate keys in sorted order
Option B: You must merge iterators across the memtable and many overlapping SSTables
Option C: Range scans always replay the WAL
Option D: Bloom filters block sequential access

Question: Why can LSM ingest a flood of random keys faster than a B-tree of similar durable settings?
Option A: User writes append to WAL and memtable instead of randomly updating leaf pages
Option B: LSM engines never fsync
Option C: B-trees cannot store random keys
Option D: Compaction is free and instantaneous

Question: Why do B-trees typically win on short range scans of nearby keys?
Option A: Leaf pages keep keys in sorted on-disk order with little file overlap, often with sibling links
Option B: They never split pages
Option C: They attach a bloom filter to every leaf
Option D: They keep all data only in memory

Question: Why do LSM engines almost always put a Bloom filter in front of each SSTable?
Option A: To compress keys so SSTables fit in RAM.
Option B: To skip files that definitely do not contain a key, cutting read amplification on point lookups.
Option C: To make range scans O(1).
Option D: To replace the WAL for crash recovery.

Question: Write amplification in an LSM tree is dominated by which activity?
Option A: Bloom-filter false positives
Option B: Rewriting the same live data again during compaction
Option C: B-tree page splits
Option D: Replica count in the cluster

Question: In C++, `std::move` on a local then using it again — what is actually true?
Option A: move guarantees the object is empty and safe to read as 0.
Option B: The object is in a valid but unspecified state; using it without reassignment is a logic bug.
Option C: move copies if the type has a destructor.
Option D: move is a runtime memcpy of the bytes only.

Question: In C++, a `std::vector<bool>` is returned and you take a reference to an element. Why is this type a famous trap?
Option A: vector<bool> is a bit-packed proxy; references/pointers to elements are not real bool&.
Option B: bool cannot live in a vector.
Option C: vector<bool> is faster and always the right default.
Option D: It is the only vector that does not reallocate.

Question: In C++, when should you prefer `unique_ptr` over `shared_ptr`?
Option A: Always use shared_ptr; unique_ptr cannot be returned from functions.
Option B: When one owner is enough: unique_ptr is cheaper (no control block/atomics) and makes ownership obvious.
Option C: unique_ptr cannot hold arrays, so shared_ptr is required for buffers.
Option D: shared_ptr is always lock-free and therefore faster.

Question: In C++, why is RAII (owning a resource in an object whose destructor releases it) the default answer to leaks and lock-forget bugs?
Option A: Destructors run on every control-flow exit from the scope, including exceptions, so release is tied to lifetime.
Option B: The compiler inserts garbage collection for RAII types.
Option C: RAII disables exceptions, so you cannot forget a catch.
Option D: new/delete become undefined if any class has a destructor.

Question: In C++, why is `std::string_view` pointing at a temporary `std::string` a dangling-view bug?
Option A: string_view copies the characters, so it cannot dangle.
Option B: string_view does not own the buffer; when the temporary dies the view is invalid.
Option C: Temporaries live until the process exits.
Option D: string_view is illegal on temporaries and will not compile.

Question: In C++, you `new` an object and `delete` it in some return paths but not after an early `return` on error. What is the RAII alternative?
Option A: Wrap the pointer in unique_ptr so the destructor deletes on every exit path.
Option B: Add more comments on the delete.
Option C: Use a raw pointer and a finally keyword.
Option D: Disable exceptions so early returns cannot happen.

Question: In C++, you compile without `-Wall` and ignore a `return` missing on one path. What class of bug is that?
Option A: A style issue with defined behavior (returns 0).
Option B: Undefined behavior: falling off a non-void function.
Option C: The compiler inserts throw.
Option D: C++ requires all paths to return, so this cannot compile.

Question: In C++, you include a using-directive `using namespace std;` in a header. Why is that a problem?
Option A: std cannot be used in headers.
Option B: Every translation unit that includes it gets std dumped into the global namespace, causing name clashes.
Option C: It disables ADL.
Option D: Headers cannot have using-declarations of any kind.

Question: In C++, you store pointers to vector elements, then `push_back` until capacity grows. What happened?
Option A: Pointers remain valid because vector is contiguous.
Option B: Reallocation invalidates pointers/iterators into the old buffer (undefined behavior if you use them).
Option C: vector is a linked structure, so pointers always stay valid.
Option D: push_back is illegal while pointers exist; it will not compile.

Question: In Cassandra, LWTs (lightweight transactions / IF clauses) are expensive mainly because they…
Option A: Skip the commit log
Option B: Run a Paxos-style round of agreement instead of a regular quorum write
Option C: Store extra bloom filters
Option D: Disable compaction

Question: In Cassandra, RF=3 and you write with CL=ONE. A client then reads with CL=ONE from a different replica. What can happen?
Option A: The read is guaranteed to see the write because ONE always hits the leader.
Option B: The read may miss the write: ONE only waits for one replica, which might not be the one that stored the write yet.
Option C: Cassandra will block the read until all replicas have the write.
Option D: CL=ONE automatically upgrades to QUORUM for the next read.

Question: In Cassandra, if RF=3 and you choose CL=ALL, what availability tradeoff did you make?
Option A: You can tolerate one replica down
Option B: Any one replica down makes the request fail, in exchange for seeing all copies
Option C: Writes become local-only
Option D: Hints are no longer stored

Question: In Cassandra, replication factor (RF) vs consistency level (CL): which statement is accurate?
Option A: RF is how many replicas store a partition; CL is how many replicas must respond for this read or write
Option B: They are the same setting with two names
Option C: CL decides where data is stored; RF decides how many acknowledgements you wait for
Option D: RF only applies to reads; CL only applies to writes

Question: In Cassandra, the coordinator node in a write path is responsible for…
Option A: Storing the only copy of the data
Option B: Sending the mutation to the replica set and waiting for CL acknowledgements
Option C: Choosing a new partition key
Option D: Running repair before every write

Question: In Cassandra, what do clustering columns control?
Option A: Which datacenter gets the write
Option B: Sort order of rows within a partition on disk and in queries
Option C: The replication factor
Option D: Whether hinted handoff is enabled

Question: In Cassandra, what does repair (anti-entropy) try to fix?
Option A: Hot partitions by splitting tokens automatically
Option B: Replicas that have diverged because of missed writes, downtime, or missed hints
Option C: The need for a partition key
Option D: Tombstone creation

Question: In Cassandra, what is hinted handoff for?
Option A: Speeding up range scans
Option B: The coordinator stores a hint when a replica is down, then replays it when the replica returns
Option C: Choosing the partition key
Option D: Replacing anti-entropy repair entirely

Question: In Cassandra, why is a full-table scan (ALLOW FILTERING / unbounded partition scan) a junior anti-pattern?
Option A: Cassandra cannot read more than one row
Option B: Data is partitioned by token; a cluster-wide scan fans out and can overwhelm many nodes
Option C: QUORUM forbids scans
Option D: Tombstones cannot be read

Question: In Cassandra, why should a partition not grow without bound (wide partition)?
Option A: Clustering order breaks after a few rows
Option B: Compaction, repair, caching, and reads of that partition concentrate work on one token and huge SSTable pieces
Option C: RF becomes 1 automatically
Option D: QUORUM cannot count replicas for wide partitions

Question: In Cassandra, with RF=3, what does a QUORUM write mean?
Option A: All 3 replicas must acknowledge
Option B: At least 2 replicas must acknowledge (majority of RF)
Option C: Only the coordinator stores the write
Option D: Exactly 1 replica must acknowledge

Question: In Cassandra, you need to fetch a user's last 100 events in time order. How should that be modeled?
Option A: Partition key = event id, so every event is its own partition for even load.
Option B: Partition key = user id, clustering key = event time, so one partition holds an ordered slice you can range-read.
Option C: A single partition for the whole table named `events` so ORDER BY always works globally.
Option D: Store events in a Cassandra collection column and let CQL sort them at query time across nodes.

Question: In Cassandra, you write at CL=ONE and later read at CL=ONE. Why might you miss your own write?
Option A: Cassandra never reads your own writes
Option B: The read may hit a replica that has not received the write yet
Option C: ONE always waits for all replicas
Option D: Tombstones block all reads at ONE

Question: What does the partition key actually control in Cassandra?
Option A: The on-disk sort order of rows inside a partition
Option B: Which node(s) own the data: it hashes to a token and thus a replica set
Option C: The consistency level of the query
Option D: Whether a bloom filter is used

Question: What is a tombstone in Cassandra?
Option A: A backup of a deleted SSTable
Option B: A deletion marker that must be stored and compacted away later so old values do not resurrect
Option C: A hint stored on a coordinator
Option D: A repair session identifier

Question: Why can a hot partition ruin a Cassandra cluster even when total QPS looks modest?
Option A: One token/partition is owned by a small replica set, so those nodes take all the load for that key
Option B: Cassandra cannot store large partitions
Option C: QUORUM is disabled for hot keys
Option D: Bloom filters stop working on busy nodes

Question: Why is DELETE in Cassandra not the same as 'the row is gone now'?
Option A: Deletes are stored as tombstones and kept until gc_grace so repair does not resurrect the row.
Option B: Cassandra cannot delete; you can only TTL the whole table.
Option C: DELETE drops the SSTable file immediately, which is why deletes are fast.
Option D: Deletes require a QUORUM of all clusters worldwide.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, DFS vs BFS for 'does a path exist in a huge, deep, narrow maze if you are memory-constrained'?
Option A: DFS uses stack proportional to depth, which can be smaller than BFS's frontier in a wide graph — but it can also go infinitely deep without extra guards
Option B: BFS always uses less memory than DFS
Option C: They use identical memory on every graph
Option D: Only union-find can test connectivity

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says 'this user id is not in the set.' What can you conclude?
Option A: It is definitely not in the set — Bloom filters have false positives, not false negatives (for a static membership filter)
Option B: It might still be in the set; negatives are probabilistic
Option C: You must re-hash with a tree to confirm negatives
Option D: The filter is corrupted whenever it says no

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says 'yes, this email was seen.' You skip sending. Risk?
Option A: False positive — you may skip a never-seen email; if skips are costly, store a real set or a cache in front of source of truth
Option B: False negative — Bloom filters invent missing emails
Option C: Union-find will correct it on the next hop
Option D: LRU will convert the maybe into a no

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says a user id is 'not present'. How should you treat that?
Option A: It might be a false negative; check the database anyway.
Option B: Trust it: Bloom filters have false positives, not false negatives (for the items actually inserted).
Option C: It is a cache, so 'not present' means 'evicted', not 'absent'.
Option D: Bloom filters only work for strings, not ids.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, an LRU cache is hit on every request for a hot key. What must the structure do in O(1) expected time?
Option A: Hash map to the node plus a recency list (or equivalent) so lookup, move-to-front, and eviction of the tail are cheap
Option B: Scan the whole array to find the oldest timestamp
Option C: Rebuild a heap from scratch on every hit
Option D: BFS the keyspace

Question: In data structures and algorithms, consistent hashing places both keys and nodes on a ring. A node dies. What should happen to its keys?
Option A: They move to the next node(s) on the ring (or to replicas), not to a random reshuffle of the whole keyspace
Option B: Every key is rehashed with % (N-1)
Option C: A Bloom filter deletes the node
Option D: LRU evicts all keys cluster-wide

Question: In data structures and algorithms, why do textbook linked-list queues often lose to a ring buffer of the same logical operations on real hardware?
Option A: Each node is a separate allocation; pointer chasing misses cache and TLB, while a contiguous buffer hits cache lines and prefetches
Option B: Linked lists have worse big-O for enqueue than arrays in the RAM model
Option C: CPUs cannot follow pointers at all
Option D: The kernel refuses to allocate list nodes

Question: In data structures and algorithms, why is a linked list usually the wrong 'insert in the middle is O(1)' answer on real hardware?
Option A: Pointer chasing destroys cache locality; an array/vector often wins even if Big-O looks worse.
Option B: Linked lists cannot insert in the middle.
Option C: The OS forbids heap-allocated nodes in user space.
Option D: CPUs execute linked-list code in O(n^2) regardless of length.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you add a cache node and want existing keys to mostly stay put. Why not hash(key) % N?
Option A: Changing N remaps almost every key; consistent hashing (or Rendezvous) moves only a ~1/N fraction
Option B: Modulo is cryptographically unsafe, so caches reject it
Option C: % N cannot be computed for strings
Option D: Heaps cannot store the modulus

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you have n chat rooms and union operations 'merge these two rooms' plus 'are these users in the same room?' Which structure?
Option A: Union-find (disjoint-set) with path compression / union by rank
Option B: A max-heap of room ids
Option C: BFS from user 0 on every query
Option D: A Bloom filter of pairs

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you iterate a large array of structs vs a linked list of the same structs, summing one field. Why is the array usually much faster?
Option A: Sequential access prefetches; the list jumps to heap allocations that evict useful cache lines
Option B: Arrays have better big-O for a linear scan than lists
Option C: Linked lists cannot store structs
Option D: The compiler forbids summing list nodes

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need 'get user by id' at huge QPS, ids are arbitrary strings, no range queries. Which shape fits the workload?
Option A: Hash table (average O(1) point lookup) — a tree adds comparison overhead you do not need, a heap is not a dictionary
Option B: Binary heap, because it always stores the minimum id on top
Option C: Linked list, because pointers are faster than arrays
Option D: DFS forest, because ids form a graph

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need O(1) expected lookup by id and do not need ordered iteration. What is the default structure, and when does it bite you?
Option A: Balanced BST: lookups are O(1).
Option B: Hash table: great until a bad hash, huge load factor, or you need range queries / sorted order.

Option B: Without flush and compaction, recovery time, file count, and obsolete versions grow without bound
Option C: Memtables cannot hold more than one key
Option D: Bloom filters cannot be built from SSTables

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, write amplification in an LSM is high. Compaction is always running. What is the engine spending I/O on?
Option A: Rewriting the same keys into new sorted runs as they age through levels, plus dropping tombstones.
Option B: Updating B-tree leaf pointers on every write.
Option C: Rebuilding Bloom filters for the WAL.
Option D: fsync of the memtable on every GET.

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, you flush tiny memtables very frequently. What is the likely first-order effect?
Option A: Lower write amplification because files are small
Option B: Many overlapping SSTables, worse read amplification, and more compaction work later
Option C: Bloom filters become exact
Option D: Range scans no longer need merge iterators

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, you need both fast random writes and efficient large range scans. What is the honest tradeoff to explain?
Option A: LSM favors ingest; scans pay merge cost across runs. B-trees favor locality; ingest pays random page writes
Option B: One structure always wins both, so pick either
Option C: Bloom filters make LSM scans as cheap as B-tree scans
Option D: Compaction removes the need to think about scans

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, you undersize bloom filters so the false-positive rate is high. What happens to LSM point-read amplification?
Option A: Nothing; bloom filters are only used in compaction
Option B: More SSTables are opened and their indexes probed even though the key is absent
Option C: Range scans become cheaper
Option D: The WAL grows faster

Question: Why can a B-tree still beat LSM on a point get even when LSM has bloom filters?
Option A: A well-cached B-tree often needs one leaf I/O (plus a few internal nodes), while LSM may still miss cache on several files
Option B: B-trees never touch disk
Option C: Bloom filters always return false
Option D: LSM cannot store point keys

Question: A data race on a non-atomic int is 'just a torn read' — why is that the wrong mental model in C++?
Option A: Data races are defined to return the last write.
Option B: A data race is undefined behavior: the compiler may miscompile the surrounding code, not merely tear the int.
Option C: The memory model only applies to atomics, so racy ints are always fine.
Option D: POSIX threads make all ints atomic.

Question: A template is defined only in a .cpp file. Other TUs that use it fail to link. Why?
Option A: Templates cannot be in cpp files ever.
Option B: The compiler needs the definition visible at instantiation, or you must explicit-instantiate; otherwise the linker cannot find the specialization.
Option C: You forgot `export template` which C++20 always requires.
Option D: The ODR allows one cpp to serve all TUs automatically.

Question: In C++, a `std::function` callback captures `this` and is stored after the object dies. What is the failure?
Option A: std::function extends the object's lifetime.
Option B: A dangling `this`; the callback is a use-after-free when invoked. Own the callback lifetime or capture what you need by value.
Option C: Lambdas cannot capture this.
Option D: The compiler rejects storing such functions.

Question: In C++, exception from a destructor during stack unwinding. What does the language do?
Option A: It nested-catches the new exception.
Option B: If a destructor throws while another exception is in flight, the process calls std::terminate.
Option C: Destructors cannot throw by language rule, so this is a compile error.
Option D: The original exception is replaced silently.

Question: In C++, shared_ptr copies in a tight loop show up in profiles. What are you paying for?
Option A: A mutex on every dereference of `*ptr`.

Option C: Virtual dispatch on every copy.
Option D: shared_ptr copies are free after inlining.

Question: In C++, you need a concurrent queue. Rolling your own with one mutex is 'too slow', so you write a lock-free queue. What should you fear first?
Option A: Lock-free is always faster and easier to prove.
Option B: ABA, memory-order mistakes, and UB that only reproduces on the other CPU; a mutex queue is often the right first product.

Option D: The standard provides a portable lock-free queue you must use.

Question: In C++, you pass a `std::initializer_list` that you stored for later. Why can it dangle?
Option A: initializer_list is a pair of pointers into a temporary array whose lifetime is the full expression.
Option B: initializer_list owns a vector.

Option D: The backing array is in static storage.

Question: You return a `std::vector` by value. Why is that usually the right API in modern C++?
Option A: It always heap-allocates twice; callers should pass an output pointer.
Option B: NRVO/move make it cheap; returning by value states ownership clearly vs a raw pointer.
Option C: vector cannot be moved.
Option D: Return-by-value copies every time before C++23 only.

Question: An LSM-style memtable flush in Cassandra is most analogous to which cost you already pay in the storage engine?
Option A: Token hashing

Option C: Gossip heartbeats
Option D: Native CQL parsing

Question: In Cassandra, LOCAL_QUORUM vs QUORUM in a multi-DC cluster: what did you change?

Option B: You wait for a majority in the local DC only, not a cluster-wide majority, cutting cross-DC latency
Option C: Tombstone gc grace
Option D: The number of clustering columns

Question: In Cassandra, LWT on a hot partition is especially painful because…
Option A: Paxos storage is on a different cluster

Option C: LWT disables the partitioner
Option D: LWT requires RF=1

Question: In Cassandra, a coordinator stores many hints for a down replica. What operational risk follows?
Option A: Hints improve read latency forever
Option B: Hint replay can storm the recovering node, and hints can expire so divergence remains until repair
Option C: The down replica is removed from RF automatically
Option D: LWT becomes free

Question: In Cassandra, a partition for one customer grew to tens of GB. Queries to that customer are slow even at CL=ONE. What is the structural problem?
Option A: CL=ONE cannot read large partitions; you must use ALL.
Option B: The whole partition is the unit of co-location; one huge partition is a single-node hotspot and a wide-row read tax.
Option C: Cassandra automatically splits partitions at 100 MB, so this cannot happen.

Question: In Cassandra, a query with no restriction on partition key but a clustering-column filter is slow. Why?
Option A: Clustering filters require LWT
Option B: Without a partition key, Cassandra cannot target a replica set; it must scatter or reject/filter broadly
Option C: Bloom filters only work on clustering columns
Option D: QUORUM cannot be used without clustering columns

Question: In Cassandra, for RF=3, why is write QUORUM + read QUORUM the classic 'strong enough' pairing?
Option A: It contacts every node in the cluster
Option B: W+R>RF so the read set and write set must overlap on at least one replica

Question: In Cassandra, range deletes and TTL expiry create many tombstones. Which read is most likely to time out?
Option A: A point get of a live key in a tiny partition with no deletes
Option B: A slice scan that must walk and skip huge runs of tombstones before finding live rows
Option C: A LOCAL_QUORUM write
Option D: A schema-agreement check

Question: In Cassandra, read repair vs full/incremental anti-entropy repair: how should you think about them?
Option A: They are identical background jobs
Option B: Read repair may fix replicas touched by a query; anti-entropy repair walks token ranges to reconcile even cold data
Option C: Read repair rewrites the schema
Option D: Anti-entropy repair only runs on the coordinator's memtable

Question: In Cassandra, repair has not run for longer than gc_grace_seconds after many deletes. What resurrection bug are you exposed to?
Option A: Tombstones expired while a replica still has the old data; repair can copy the old row back.

Question: In Cassandra, why can hinted handoff not replace repair?
Option A: Hints only cover some missed writes for a limited window; they do not reconcile all replica divergence
Option B: Hints always corrupt data
Option C: Repair cannot run if hints exist
Option D: Hints only work at CL=ALL

Question: In Cassandra, why is 'RF=3, CL=QUORUM, but NetworkTopologyStrategy with RF=3 in only one DC' a different failure domain than two DCs of RF=3?
Option A: It is not; RF is global

Question: In Cassandra, you model 'all events for a user' as partition=user_id, clustering=time. What hot-partition pattern should you expect?
Option A: Users are perfectly balanced by definition

Question: In Cassandra, you write QUORUM and read QUORUM with RF=3. Why is this still not a linearizable compare-and-set for two clients updating the same cell?
Option A: QUORUM already provides linearizability for all writes.

Option D: Cassandra serializes all writes to a partition through a single leader like Raft.

Question: Why does Cassandra still need gc_grace-style delay before dropping tombstones?
Option A: To keep bloom filters warm

Option C: QUORUM counts tombstones as live votes
Option D: LWTs require tombstones forever

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a UI table sorts by selected column. Rows with equal values jump around every click. Users complain. Fix?
Option A: Use a stable sort, or add a hidden unique tie-breaker (original index) so the order is deterministic
Option B: Switch from array to linked list of rows
Option C: BFS the table model
Option D: Put rows in a Bloom filter

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a priority queue of tasks also needs 'cancel task by id.' Plain binary heap problem?
Option A: Find-by-id is not a heap operation — keep a hash from id → heap index (or a tree of tasks) so decrease-key/delete is possible

Question: In data structures and algorithms, an LRU cache is a hash map plus a doubly linked list. Why both?
Option A: The list gives O(1) lookup; the map gives recency.
Option B: The map finds the node in O(1); the list moves that node to most-recent in O(1) and evicts the tail in O(1).
Option C: The map is only for persistence; LRU can be a list alone in O(1).
Option D: A heap would be strictly better for LRU.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, bloom filter at 1% false positive, you then always fetch the DB on 'yes.' What did you actually save?
Option A: Negative lookups skip the DB; positives (true and false) still pay the DB round trip — win is skewed to mostly-miss workloads

Question: In data structures and algorithms, cache with consistent hashing. Client hashes to node A; A misses and fills from DB. Node A is added/removed and the key now lives on B, which is empty. User-visible issue?

Option B: Consistent hashing forbids misses after a membership change
Option C: LRU on B automatically contains A's memory
Option D: Bloom filters migrate the bytes

Question: In data structures and algorithms, consistent hashing without virtual nodes, 3 physical caches of unequal capacity. Typical pain?

Option B: All keys hash to node 0 by definition
Option C: Union-find is required to split the ring
Option D: LRU cannot run on a ring

Question: In data structures and algorithms, consistent hashing without virtual nodes: one cache host dies. Why is the remap worse than it should be?
Option A: All keys must move to a random new host, not just the dead one's.

Option C: Consistent hashing requires a coordinator to rewrite every key.
Option D: Dead nodes keep their keys until a full rehash.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, graph of a social network: find people within 2 hops. Why BFS beats DFS here?

Option C: BFS cannot handle cycles

Question: In data structures and algorithms, hash table vs balanced tree for a language runtime dictionary. Hash is faster on average. When do you still pick the tree?

Option B: Trees always beat hashes on point lookup
Option C: Heaps iterate in hash order
Option D: Linked lists iterate faster than both

Question: In data structures and algorithms, kruskal-style clustering: merge closest pairs until k clusters. Why union-find instead of rerunning DFS?
Option A: Each merge and 'same cluster?' is cheap with disjoint sets; DFS from scratch every edge is repeating connectivity work
Option B: DFS cannot detect connected components
Option C: Heaps find components faster than union-find
Option D: Bloom filters cluster by hash collisions on purpose

Option A: Store subtree/component size on the root; union by size and add sizes on merge — queries read the root's size after find
Option B: Run BFS from every node after each union
Option C: Put components in a max-heap keyed by an arbitrary id
Option D: Hash each pair of nodes

Question: In data structures and algorithms, workload: 10M keys, need 'all keys between A and B' and occasional insert. Engineer proposes a hash map. What fails?

Option B: A heap of URLs ordered by length

Option A: Each idle-in-transaction backend holds a snapshot, preventing xmin advancement, vacuum, and releasing of catalog caches tied to that snapshot
Option B: Idle-in-transaction sessions do not use a backend process
Option C: PostgreSQL automatically sets synchronous_commit = off for idle transactions
Option D: WAL is fsynced continuously for idle snapshots

Question: In PostgreSQL, a multi-master-like design uses logical replication with conflict avoidance by partitioning key ranges per node. An UPDATE moves a row across ranges. What breaks?
Option A: The UPDATE is not a DELETE+INSERT across publications, so the row can vanish or duplicate depending on replica identity and filters
Option B: PostgreSQL converts the UPDATE into a HOT update on the subscriber automatically
Option C: WAL is not generated for cross-range updates
Option D: synchronous_commit ignores logical slots for such rows

Question: In PostgreSQL, a multi-tenant SaaS puts all tenants in one cluster. One tenant runs analytical queries that blow up work_mem and temp files. What isolation strategy actually protects neighbors?
Option A: A single `statement_timeout` equal for everyone is enough.
Option B: Separate roles/pools with memory/timeouts, plus (if needed) separate databases or clusters; Postgres does not give hard multi-tenant CPU isolation inside one instance.
Option C: MVCC isolates CPU as well as row versions.
Option D: Put the noisy tenant on a replica and they cannot affect the primary's CPU.

Question: In PostgreSQL, a partial index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL becomes huge despite few live rows. What went wrong?
Option A: Updates that set deleted_at still leave index entries for old MVCC versions until vacuum; a long xmin horizon prevents cleanup
Option B: Partial indexes index every row regardless of predicate
Option C: IS NULL predicates cannot be used in partial indexes
Option D: HOT updates duplicate partial index entries on purpose

Question: In PostgreSQL, a query uses a GiST index on a range type. Concurrent updates cause a lot of page splits. Which correctness vs performance tension exists?
Option A: GiST must maintain balanced predicate trees under MVCC, so splits WAL-log internal pages and can bloat faster than btree on overlapping ranges
Option B: GiST updates are never WAL-logged, risking replica divergence
Option C: GiST ignores isolation levels by design
Option D: VACUUM cannot recycle GiST pages without REINDEX CONCURRENTLY plus a restart

Question: In PostgreSQL, a standby is used for read scaling. A long reporting query on the standby conflicts with WAL replay of a VACUUM that wants to remove tuples still visible to the query. What happens if hot_standby_feedback is off and max_standby_streaming_delay is short?
Option A: The standby cancels the query so replay can proceed, or replay waits then cancels—reads are sacrificed to keep apply moving
Option B: The primary automatically delays VACUUM until the standby query ends, with no configuration
Option C: The standby silently returns wrong results for removed tuples
Option D: HOT chains are rebuilt on the standby without canceling queries

Question: In PostgreSQL, connection poolers (PgBouncer) in transaction pooling hide session state. Which app pattern silently breaks?
Option A: Simple prepared statements that last one transaction.
Option B: Session-level features: SET, temp tables, WITH HOLD cursors, advisory locks you expected to last the HTTP connection.
Option C: Read-only queries.
Option D: Using a single user role.

Question: In PostgreSQL, during a crash recovery, redo is slow because of a huge uncheckpointed WAL volume after a bulk load with few checkpoints. What is the trade-off you mis-set?
Option A: High max_wal_size / checkpoint_timeout reduced checkpoint I/O during the load but lengthened crash recovery
Option B: synchronous_commit = off disables redo entirely
Option C: full_page_writes = on prevents recovery from using WAL
Option D: HOT updates cannot be redone, so recovery rebuilds indexes from scratch

Question: In PostgreSQL, full_page_writes is on (default). After a checkpoint, the first change to a page writes a full page image. How does this interact with a storage that already does atomic 8K writes?
Option A: You still pay WAL amplification to protect against torn pages on typical hardware; turning it off is only safe on systems that guarantee atomic page writes
Option B: full_page_writes is redundant with MVCC and can always be off
Option C: full_page_writes only applies to indexes, not heap
Option D: Replicas ignore full page images and reconstruct pages from btree

Question: In PostgreSQL, hash partitioning vs range partitioning for a multi-tenant id. Queries always filter by tenant_id. Why might hash still be the wrong choice at staff scale?
Option A: You cannot drop a tenant by detaching one partition; data for one tenant is scattered, so retention and locality suffer
Option B: Hash partitions cannot have indexes
Option C: The planner cannot prune hash partitions even with equality on the partition key
Option D: HOT updates are impossible on hash partitions

Question: In PostgreSQL, hot_standby_feedback = on protects standby queries from replay conflict. What cost does the primary pay?
Option A: Vacuum on the primary cannot remove tuples still needed by standby snapshots, so bloat and wraparound risk grow with long standby queries
Option B: The primary disables HOT updates
Option C: synchronous_commit is forced to remote_apply
Option D: Indexes on the primary cannot be used until feedback ACKs

Question: In PostgreSQL, on a huge append-only table, aggressive autovacuum still scans endlessly. What freeze/visibility-map strategy actually reduces that work?
Option A: Insert-only vacuum and freezing new pages so the visibility map stays all-visible and future vacuums skip them
Option B: Disable freeze because append-only tables never wrap XIDs
Option C: Create more btree indexes so vacuum can skip the heap
Option D: Set synchronous_commit = off to skip freezing

Question: In PostgreSQL, synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ: commits now wait on the network. A failover-happy load balancer flaps the standby. What failure did you couple into the write path?
Option A: None; sync replica loss is ignored until you promote.
Option B: Commits stall or fail when the sync standby is unhealthy; you bought durability/availability of the standby into every write's latency SLO.
Option C: PostgreSQL automatically falls back to local commits with the same RPO.
Option D: The primary buffers sync commits in shared buffers indefinitely.

Question: In PostgreSQL, you enable checksums after seeing silent corruption on a replica. What operational cost is now permanent?
Option A: Every heap/index page read verifies checksums and writes pay to maintain them, adding CPU; enabling later still requires a rewrite of all files
Option B: Checksums replace WAL, so crash recovery is skipped
Option C: Checksums only apply when synchronous_commit is off
Option D: MVCC visibility is stored in checksums instead of hint bits

Question: In PostgreSQL, you need close-to-zero downtime DDL on a 10 TB table (add a column with a non-constant default, historically). What is the staff-level instinct?
Option A: Run it in a transaction on the primary during peak; MVCC makes it instant.
Option B: Treat it as an expand/contract migration: add nullable column, backfill in batches, then constrain — not one blocking rewrite if the version still rewrites.
Option C: Logical replication ignores table rewrites, so just ALTER.
Option D: Global indexes make any DDL O(1).

Question: In PostgreSQL, you observe subtransaction overflow (pg_subtrans) under a PL/pgSQL loop of SAVEPOINTs. What is the failure mode?
Option A: Hint-bit and snapshot checks degrade because subxids no longer fit in the in-memory cache, causing pg_subtrans I/O
Option B: WAL is discarded for nested subtransactions
Option C: HOT updates are forced for every SAVEPOINT
Option D: The backend switches isolation to READ UNCOMMITTED

Question: You are choosing between a huge partitioned table with a global unique constraint vs uniqueness in the application. PostgreSQL unique indexes are per partition (unless you include the partition key). What is the real design constraint?
Option A: Global uniqueness is free if you use logical replication.
Option B: A unique index can only guarantee uniqueness within the index's scope; cross-partition uniqueness needs the partition key in the constraint or an external allocator.
Option C: Partitioning always preserves all unique constraints of the parent with no extra columns.
Option D: Unique constraints are enforced by WAL, which is global.

Question: You need zero-downtime DDL that rewrites a table (type change). Why is CREATE TABLE new + concurrent backfill + swap still hard in PostgreSQL?
Option A: In-flight writes, identity/serial sequences, FK/triggers, and logical replica identity must be dual-written or locked around cutover or rows are lost
Option B: PostgreSQL cannot CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the new table
Option C: MVCC prevents INSERT into two tables in one transaction
Option D: WAL cannot contain both old and new row formats

Question: A scientific team wants to run a 32-core CPU-bound pipeline in one CPython process with threads. What do you change in the architecture?
Option A: Increase thread count to 256.
Option B: Use processes, a native GIL-releasing library, or another runtime; threads will not use the cores for bytecode.
Option C: Enable asyncio; it bypasses the GIL for CPU.
Option D: The GIL is gone for CPU loops if you `await` them.

Question: In Python, a data pipeline pickles pandas objects between steps. After a pandas upgrade, workers cannot read old files. What was the architectural mistake?
Option A: pandas objects cannot be serialized.
Option B: Pickle is an in-process, version-fragile format; a durable pipeline wants parquet/arrow/json with a schema.
Option C: You should have used `eval`.
Option D: Pickle is schema-stable across pandas majors.

Question: In Python, a native C extension allocates GIL-holding work for 50ms per request. How do you get concurrency back?
Option A: Add more threads; the GIL will schedule them during the 50ms.
Option B: Release the GIL in the extension around the heavy work, or move it out of process; otherwise threads buy nothing.
Option C: asyncio.wait will interleave C code.
Option D: Set `PYTHONTHREADSAWARE=1`.

Question: In Python, a web worker pool + a background thread that mutates a dict without locks. GIL makes this 'safe', right?
Option A: Yes; GIL serializes all bytecode so dicts are atomic for any compound update.
Option B: No; GIL can interleave bytecode between operations; dict compound updates still need locks or a queue to a single owner thread.
Option C: dicts are immutable in CPython.
Option D: Only list.append needs a lock.

Question: In Python, subinterpreters / free-threading are on the table. What still has to be true of your C extensions?
Option A: They are automatically safe because they used the GIL once.
Option B: They must be explicit about shared state; many extensions still assume a single interpreter and a GIL.
Option C: All PyPI wheels are already free-threaded.
Option D: Only the stdlib needs changes; extensions cannot share objects.

Question: In Python, you must hot-reload code in a long-lived worker. Why is `importlib.reload` a staff-level last resort?
Option A: reload cannot fail.
Option B: Old objects, class identities, and singletons survive; you get mixed versions and leaking modules. Prefer rolling new processes.
Option C: reload is the same as restarting the interpreter.
Option D: CPython forbids reload in production by raising.

Question: In Python, you must ship a tool to air-gapped machines. What packaging failure mode should you design against?
Option A: wheels always contain every manylinux ABI.
Option B: Native deps, implicit system libraries, and 'pip install from PyPI' at runtime; vendoring/lock a compatible wheel set or use a frozen runtime.
Option C: CPython binaries are identical across distros.
Option D: venv is guaranteed present on all OS images.

Question: A 'Redis transaction' across keys in different slots needs:
Option A: MULTI/EXEC only
Option B: A different design: hash tags to colocate, an external workflow, or a real database transaction — Cluster will refuse the cross-slot MULTI
Option C: RDB snapshot isolation
Option D: Pub/Sub as the commit log

Question: A platform team offers Redis as 'multi-tenant durable storage' with one cluster and no key namespaces/limits. What will happen?
Option A: Redis ACLs make noisy neighbors impossible.
Option B: One tenant's large keys, KEYS, or unbounded growth will stall or evict everyone; you need isolation (instances), maxmemory policies, and key prefixes with hard quotas.
Option C: Cluster slots isolate tenants automatically.
Option D: AOF rewrite is per key, so tenants cannot interact.

Question: In Redis, AOF rewrite and RDB fork at the same time on a memory-tight host. Operational risk?
Option A: Slots reshuffle
Option B: Double copy-on-write memory spike, latency stall, or OOM killer — persistence settings are a capacity plan, not just 'on'
Option C: Eviction turns into noeviction
Option D: Replicas become source of truth

Question: In Redis, WAIT or WAITAOF after a write is how you:
Option A: Make Redis a multi-primary consensus store
Option B: Block until replicas (or AOF) catch up to a durability bar you chose; default writes do not wait
Option C: Disable eviction globally
Option D: Rebalance slots

Question: In Redis, a cluster slot migration is in progress. Clients must handle:
Option A: A frozen keyspace with no errors
Option B: ASK/MOVED redirects and transient multi-key failures; treating Redis like a single always-local node will break
Option C: Automatic AOF merge across nodes
Option D: Synchronous replica promotion of every key

Question: In Redis, big keys (a million-member hash) hurt more than memory size because:
Option A: Cluster cannot hash them
Option B: Many commands become O(N) on the single thread (serialize, expire, replica sync, client output)
Option C: AOF cannot log hashes
Option D: Eviction skips hashes

Question: In Redis, blocking commands (BLPOP, BZPOPMIN) on a shared instance interact with the single thread how?
Option A: They run on a second GIL
Option B: They park that client, but a flood of them plus large fanout still competes for the one command loop and output buffers
Option C: They force AOF off
Option D: They rebalance slots

Question: In Redis, client-side caching / tracking exists because:
Option A: The server thread wants more KEYS calls
Option B: Even an in-memory round trip is expensive at huge QPS; local memory with invalidation beats a hot Redis key
Option C: AOF becomes optional then
Option D: Slots move to the client

Question: In Redis, hash-slot coverage after a node death: the cluster goes down for those slots unless:
Option A: AOF is always fsynced
Option B: Replicas exist for that node and failover succeeds; Redis Cluster is not magic extra durability of the data model
Option C: Eviction is LRU
Option D: Clients retry KEYS

Question: In Redis, serving cache-aside correctly means on write you:
Option A: Only SET Redis and trust eviction to notify the DB
Option B: Write the database first (or in a defined order) and invalidate/update Redis so the cache cannot resurrect stale truth
Option C: KEYS and rewrite all entries
Option D: Disable TTL so Redis becomes source of truth

Question: In Redis, streams with consumer groups beat a naive list queue when:
Option A: You need cluster-wide ACID
Option B: You need pending entries, acknowledgements, and replay after a worker crash — still not a durable business ledger by itself
Option C: You need strongly consistent GSIs
Option D: You want eviction to delete jobs first

Question: In Redis, why can pipelining + Cluster be wrong if you blindly batch keys?
Option A: Pipelines cannot send SET

Option C: Pipelines force RDB
Option D: Pipelines disable eviction mid-batch as a transaction

Question: In Redis, you need a distributed lock. Someone uses SET NX without expiry, or with expiry but no fencing token. What bug remains?
Option A: None; NX is a correct lock.
Option B: A lock can be held forever, or expire while work continues and a second worker runs — without fencing, both sides mutate the resource.
Option C: Redis locks are linearizable if you use WAIT.
Option D: Expiry is unnecessary if clients are in the same VPC.

Question: Redis is used as a session store. A replica is promoted after async replication lag. What did users just lose, and what is the staff fix?
Option A: Nothing; promotion waits for replicas.
Option B: Recent sessions/writes that never made the replica; either accept RPO, use WAIT/sync replication (latency), or don't put irreplaceable sessions only in Redis.

Question: Stampede plus a single-threaded Redis plus a slow DB fill is a cascade. A robust refill looks like:
Option A: TTL=0 on every key

Option A: Postgres is faster

Question: You observe p99 spikes every N minutes with no app deploy. A likely Redis cause is:
Option A: Cluster slots wrapping at 16384
Option B: Fork-based persistence, large expiry storms, or big-key commands — all block or stall the same thread
Option C: Eventually consistent reads
Option D: On-demand memory billing

Question: A payment service must not lose 'charge then record' if the process dies after HTTP 200 from Stripe. What Spring-centric pattern actually works?
Option A: @Transactional around the Stripe SDK call.

Option C: @Async so the charge happens after response.

Question: In Spring Boot, two Boot services share a database and Hibernate entities. Why do staff platform teams fight this?
Option A: Hibernate cannot map the same table twice in the world.
Option B: You coupled deployability and schemas: migrations, locks, and incompatible entity changes become a distributed monolith. Split data ownership.
Option C: Spring forbids two apps on one JDBC URL.

Question: In Spring Boot, you inherited a monolith Boot app that starts a full context for every integration test. CI is 40 minutes. What is the staff testing strategy?
Option A: Only @SpringBootTest; slicing hides bugs.
